judge.label: LLM rubric score, fresh-context judge, self-assessed — not human QA.
judge.independence_caveat: This judge is a different model family and a fresh context: it saw only the judge prompt, the rubric and the lesson. It did not direct the project and did not author anything in it. It is still a language model scoring a language model's output, so the label applies: not human QA.

notes.bilingual_quality: The lesson declares bilingual: true, but every *Ar field — title, body, definition cards, worked example, scenario, takeaways, and both knowledge-check items with all feedback — contains the identical English text as the *En field. There is no Arabic on the page to assess; this is below even 'a literal rendering of English word order'. Scored 1 against the lesson's own bilingual declaration, per the applicability note.
notes.accessibility_ip: Compliant on IP: no licensed code descriptors, payer policy text, or denylisted terms, and no colour-only meaning. Held at 3 because there is nothing beyond compliance — no images or alt text present, and the opportunity to use the regime-neutral drafting ('in most regimes') as an explicit teaching point about jurisdiction-dependence is left implicit.

verdict_notes: In English this is a strong lesson: the worked example reasons through a real decision, the knowledge-check distractors are drawn from live misconceptions, and the autocomplete scenario has genuine friction. But the bilingual declaration is unmet in the most literal sense — every Arabic field is English — so bilingual_quality is a 1. Mean 4.0 with one criterion below the floor; the gate decides.
